\title{Measuring Complex Tastes: A Multiple Factor Analysis of Preferences, Consumption, and Evaluations in Musical Taste}

\author{Omar Lizardo\\ \small University of California, Los Angeles} \date{October 2026}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent This paper proposes an approach to measuring complex tastes in data that include preferences, engagement, and evaluations of the same set of objects, whether genre categories or specific cultural objects. I take a Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) approach based on Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA). The method lets us answer concrete substantive questions about complex tastes, including whether preferences, engagement, and evaluations are equally potent determinants of complex tastes, and whether some complex taste dimensions relate more or less to others. In addition, the method captures the duality of complex tastes: individuals are more or less likely to be sources of complex tastes (some individuals have simple tastes, others more complex ones), and genres/objects are more or less likely to be targets (with some genres being more likely to have simple versus complex taste profiles). I demonstrate the approach's utility using data on Americans' complex tastes for twenty musical genres collected circa 2012.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Sociologists measure cultural taste in at least three distinct ways \citep{ma2026tastes}. One tradition takes taste to be a \emph{preference}---a person's affective response toward a cultural object. A second takes taste to be an orientation toward \emph{consumption}---realized participation or engagement within a cultural field. A third takes taste to be a faculty expressed in \emph{valuations}---judgments about the quality or status of cultural objects. Rather than treating this semantic ambiguity as a defect to be resolved by fiat, \citet{ma2026tastes} argues that taste should be conceptualized pluralistically as a person's ``thick subjectivity'' in a cultural field: a multidimensional orientation expressed through multiple modalities of action that guides our preferences, engagement, and evaluations.

Recognizing the multimodality of taste sharpens the formulation of \emph{complex taste} phenomena. Simple tastes are those in which the modalities are harmonized: what a person likes, what they consume, and what they value point in the same direction. Complex tastes, by contrast, are configurations in which the modalities disagree---the guilty pleasure (liked and consumed but disvalued), the taste pose (liked and valued but not consumed), distanced consumption (consumed but neither liked nor valued), and their kin \citep{ma2026tastes}. Complex tastes, on this view, cannot be described by recourse to any single mode of action.

This paper develops a measurement strategy for complex tastes that takes the pluralist conception seriously. The strategy uses Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa}, a member of the Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) family used by  \citet{bourdieu1984distinction} in his classic study \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44, roux2004geometric-65c}, applied to a data structure in which each cultural object is described by three sets of indicators, one for each modality of taste. The block structure of the MFA allows us to ask the questions the theory makes salient: how strong are the links between the preference, consumption, and evaluation modalities? Do the modalities contribute equally to the shared structure of taste? And where, geometrically, do complex tastes live?

\section{Data and Measures}

\subsection{Data}

I use the Survey Sample International (SSI) 2012 Cultural Tastes Survey \citep{lizardo2012ssi}, a national sample of $N = 2{,}276$ American adults collected circa 2012. The survey contains, for each of twenty musical genres, measures of the respondent's liking of the genre, their consumption of the genre, and their perceptions of the social characteristics of the genre's typical fans. After listwise deletion of the $17$ cases with missing data on any of the $60$ analysis variables, the analytic sample contains $N = 2{,}259$ valid respondents.

\subsection{Measures: Three Modalities of Taste for Twenty Genres}

Each genre contributes three binary indicators, one per modality, yielding $20 \times 3 = 60$ variables organized into three groups of twenty.

\begin{description}
\item[Preference (liking).] Respondents rated how much they like each genre on a four-point scale (like; dislike; neither like nor dislike; not familiar). A genre is coded $1$ if the respondent likes it and $0$ otherwise; unfamiliarity is treated as non-liking, consistent with the reading that an affective response requires familiarity with the object.
\item[Consumption (engagement).] Respondents checked which of the twenty genres they had listened to in the past month ($1 = $ listened, $0 = $ otherwise).
\item[Evaluation (status valuation).] Respondents indicated, from a list of social characteristics, the attributes of the genre's \emph{typical fan}. A genre is coded $1$ if the respondent attributed high status to its typical fans---that is, if they indicated the typical fan is college educated \emph{and} either middle or upper class---and $0$ otherwise.
\end{description}

Table~\ref{tab:genre-rates} reports the proportion of respondents coded $1$ on each indicator. Overall, $41.7\%$ of genre-responses are positive on the preference measure, $22.9\%$ on consumption, and $30.3\%$ on evaluation. The conjunctive status standard is demanding---requiring both a college credential and middle- or upper-class standing---and evaluation is accordingly the least frequently affirmed modality: respondents grant conjunctive high status to a genre's fans less readily than they like the genre or have recently listened to it.

\section{Analytic Strategy}

Multiple Factor Analysis \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa} is designed for data structures of this kind: a set of individuals described by several blocks of variables measured on the same individuals, with the goal of a common representation that treats the blocks---here the three modalities of taste---as comparable without letting any one block dominate ex ante.\footnote{The MFA literature calls these sets of variables ``groups'' \citep{pages2014mfa}. We speak of \emph{blocks of variables}---or of \emph{modalities}, when referring to the three blocks of this application---reserving ``group'' for its ordinary sociological meaning.} Throughout, we use \emph{modality} for one of the three ways of measuring taste distinguished in the introduction---preference, engagement, and evaluation---each entering the analysis as its own block of twenty genre indicators. Here we analyze a table with as many rows as individuals in the data and sixty columns that designate each individual's preferences, consumption, and evaluation of twenty musical genres. The $ij^{th}$ cell in the data, corresponding to row $i$ and column $j$, equals one if individual $i$ likes, consumes, or evaluates genre $j$ highly.

MFA proceeds in two steps. First, we analyze each block of variables separately by running a separate Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) on each of the three individual-by-genre tables (20 columns and the same number of individuals), one table per modality (preference, consumption, and evaluation).\footnote{A robustness check verifies that this choice is not driving the results: re-estimating the same MFA with each block analyzed instead by a scaled PCA of the binary indicators leaves every substantive result intact. The eigenvalues agree to two decimals ($1.670$, $1.209$, and $0.895$ versus $1.667$, $1.193$, and $0.899$ on the first three dimensions); the RV structure is unchanged (preference--consumption $0.32$; evaluation--preference and evaluation--consumption $0.05$ and $0.07$); individual coordinates correlate at $0.99$, $0.99$, and $0.97$ across the first three dimensions (up to sign), and the complex-taste scores at $0.97$, $0.97$, and $0.93$; the antinomy shares of projected partial inertia are $51\%$, $52\%$, and $62\%$, against $51\%$, $51\%$, and $62\%$ in the MCA version. The one substantive difference concerns rare categories: MCA gives them proportionally more weight, stretching the most distinctive affirmations---here a feature, since the rare affirmations carry the theoretical interest.} Second, we combine the separate analyses into a global analysis, weighting each block by the inverse of the first eigenvalue of its separate analysis to ensure that all three modalities contribute comparably to the global structure, regardless of the strength of the first dimension. Here, the global structure is the ``complex taste space,'' and each separate space is a complex taste dimension (preference, engagement, and evaluation).

The MFA approach provides quantities that, in turn, answer the measurement questions posed by the study of complex tastes. The first question is whether the three modalities are redundant or partially independent; the latter is required to justify studying complex tastes in the first place. After all, if preferences contained the same information as either consumption or evaluation, then studying simple tastes based on preferences would be sufficient. The \textit{RV coefficient} between two blocks of variables (here, complex-taste modalities) is a global measure of the similarities of the geometries that two blocks impose on the same individuals---the multivariate analog of a squared correlation between two block-specific images of the respondents, running from 0 (nothing in common) to 1 (the same structure).\footnote{For each block $h$, let $\mathbf{S}_h$ be the block's configuration matrix: the matrix of weighted cross-products between respondents induced by its twenty indicators, $\mathbf{S}_h = \mathbf{Z}_h \mathbf{W}_h \mathbf{Z}_h'$, where $\mathbf{Z}_h$ is the centered indicator matrix and $\mathbf{W}_h$ holds the MCA column weights. The $(i,i')$ entry of $\mathbf{S}_h$ is large when respondents $i$ and $i'$ answer alike on that modality's twenty genres. The RV coefficient between blocks $h$ and $k$ is $\mathrm{RV}(h,k) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k) / \sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h^2)\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_k^2)}$: the cosine between the two configurations viewed as vectors of pairwise respondent similarities.} If preference, engagement, and evaluation induced similar structures, any one of them could stand in for the others, and a person's tastes could be measured as simple tastes. Small RV coefficients mean instead that each modality carries information the others lack: they establish, at the level of the data structure, the possibility of complex tastes---respondents whose modalities do not line up---before any individual is measured.

The second question is whether each modality actually participates in the common representation that the MFA builds from them. The \textit{$Lg$ coefficient} measures the strength of the link between a block of variables and the global structure: how much of the block's own geometry is expressed in the compromise.\footnote{Formally, $Lg(h,k) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k) / \sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h^2)}$: the numerator of the RV coefficient, normalized by the first block's inertia alone. Because the link is not divided by the second structure's overall strength, $Lg$ measures the association on an absolute scale, and $Lg(h,k) \neq Lg(k,h)$. $Lg(h, \mathrm{MFA})$ takes the compromise configuration $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{MFA}}$ as the second argument.} The $Lg$ coefficient assigns a single number to each modality---it asks about the modality's participation in the compromise as a whole, not about any one dimension of it---and because it is measured on an absolute scale it can be compared across modalities and against the common structure. The balancing weights ensure equal influence for the three modalities at the outset, not equal presence in the result; a modality with a much weaker internal structure could, in principle, be present in name only. The $Lg$ coefficients therefore tell us whether each of the three complex taste dimensions leaves a detectable imprint on the complex taste space, or whether the compromise quietly drops one of them.

The third question is different: not how the modalities relate to one another or to the compromise, but which modality organizes each dimension of the shared space. The \textit{modality contributions}---called \emph{group contributions} in the MFA literature---apportion each dimension of the common representation among the three modalities---the share of the dimension's variance carried by each modality.\footnote{Formally, the contribution of modality $h$ to dimension $s$ is $\mathrm{ctr}(h,s) = \sum_{j \in h} w_j f_{js}^2 / \lambda_s$: the sum over the modality's twenty variables of their weighted squared coordinates on the dimension, divided by the dimension's eigenvalue $\lambda_s$; the three modalities' contributions sum to $100\%$ on every dimension.} The contrast with the $Lg$ coefficient is worth stating plainly: the $Lg$ coefficients assign each modality one number, while the modality contributions assign each dimension one decomposition. The contributions reveal whether the axes of the taste space are jointly constituted by preference, engagement, and evaluation or are, in substance, the axis of one modality echoed in the others---whether one dimension is dominated by consumption at the expense of preference and evaluation, or is equitably defined by all three. This matters for complex tastes because a dimension dominated by a single modality---one organized by what respondents praise rather than by what they prefer or consume---is precisely where the modalities can come apart, and therefore where complex tastes should appear. 

The MFA's block structure also provides the machinery to measure complex tastes directly in the geometry of the space. In the combined representation, each individual $i$ is associated with $H$ \emph{partial points}---one per modality---whose average is the individual's global point. For a given dimension $s$, the projected partial inertia of individual $i$ decomposes exactly as
\begin{equation}
\sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)^2 \;=\; H \cdot F_s(i)^2 \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^{H} \left(F_{sh}(i) - F_s(i)\right)^2}_{W_s(i)},
\label{eq:decomp}
\end{equation}
where $F_s(i)$ is the individual's global coordinate and $F_{sh}(i)$ their partial coordinate from modality $h$. The first term locates the individual in the common space; the second, $W_s(i)$, measures how dispersed the modality-specific points are around that common position. It is zero when the three modalities place the individual identically---the geometry of a simple taste---and grows with disagreement between modalities. We therefore call $W_s(i)$ the individual's \emph{complex-taste score} on dimension $s$. The squared pairwise distances between partial points ($d^2_{\text{pref-cons}}$, $d^2_{\text{pref-eval}}$, $d^2_{\text{cons-eval}}$) further decompose $W_s(i)$ into disagreement between specific pairs of modalities.\footnote{As the discrete complement to this geometric measure, each genre--respondent pair is classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex tastes (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}).}

The decomposition is easiest to grasp with an example (Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}). Consider a respondent who likes sixteen of the twenty genres---from jazz, Broadway/show tunes, and classic rock/oldies to rap/hip-hop, top 40, and heavy metal---listens to seven of them, and credits the fans of seventeen genres with college-educated, middle- or upper-class standing. On the first dimension, the general-affirmation axis, all three modality points sit on the same side of the origin---preference at $+3.33$, consumption at $+1.41$, evaluation at $+2.56$, around a global point of $+2.43$---so the modalities disagree only about \emph{how much} this respondent engages, and only modestly: $W_1 = 1.9$, or 10\% of the projected partial inertia. The third dimension, the status-valuation axis, tells a different story. The preference and consumption points sit at $+2.27$ and $+3.58$, on the side anchored by consumption of the consecrated genres, while the evaluation point sits at $-3.53$, on the side anchored by the strict status attributions: the respondent likes and listens to jazz without crediting jazz fans with high status---a guilty pleasure---and grants high status to the fans of opera, indie and alternative rock, and heavy metal without liking or listening to those genres---distant praise. The global point is $+0.77$, and the disagreement now dwarfs the position: $W_3 = (2.27 - 0.77)^2 + (3.58 - 0.77)^2 + (-3.53 - 0.77)^2 = 28.7$, or 94\% of the projected partial inertia---nearly everything that places this respondent on the status-valuation dimension is disagreement between modalities rather than shared orientation.\footnote{In Ma's combinatorial terms (see Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}), the same respondent holds thirteen genres in complex configurations: one guilty pleasure (jazz), eight taste poses, three instances of distant praise, and one justified abstention.} The second dimension completes the illustration in a different register: the respondent's global coordinate there is nearly null ($+0.01$), with preference and consumption just on the popular side of the origin ($-0.24$ and $-0.96$) and evaluation alone on the highbrow side ($+1.24$), so that the position term almost vanishes and the disagreement---$W_2 = 2.5$---is virtually the whole of the projected partial inertia. A single summary number would miss this structure: the same respondent carries a small $W_1$ and an extreme $W_3$, which is why the complex-taste scores are reported dimension by dimension.

Colored points are the modality-specific partial points; the black diamond is the respondent's global (compromise) position, their average. Dashed segments connect each partial point to the compromise. The sum of squared horizontal deviations from the compromise is $W_1 = 1.9$ (10\% of the projected partial inertia); the sum of squared vertical deviations is $W_3 = 28.7$ (94\%).}

\section{Results}

\subsection{Overall Structure of the Taste Space}

Table~\ref{tab:eigen} reports the eigenvalue decomposition. The first dimension ($\lambda_1 = 1.67$) accounts for $12.3\%$ of the variance and the second ($\lambda_2 = 1.19$) for $8.8\%$; the first five dimensions cumulate to $37.9\%$. Percentages of this magnitude are typical for categorical GDA of sparse binary indicators, where a large share of the variance is idiosyncratic genre-by-genre variation.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Eigenvalues of the MFA (first five dimensions).}
\label{tab:eigen}
\input{tables/tab-eigen}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.75\linewidth]{fig-scree} \caption{Scree plot of the MFA. Labels give the percentage of variance explained by each dimension.}
\label{fig:scree}
\end{figure}

The category coordinates support a reading of the first two dimensions. On the first dimension, the ``yes'' categories of all three modalities are arrayed on the positive side of the origin---listening to folk ($+1.52$), bluegrass ($+1.40$), opera ($+1.16$), and reggae ($+1.08$) are the most extreme consumption affirmations---while the corresponding ``no'' categories occupy the negative side. Notably, the strict status attributions themselves number among the most distinctive affirmative positions on this axis: attributing college-educated, middle- or upper-class standing to the fans of reggae ($+1.15$), bluegrass ($+1.14$), rap/hip-hop ($+1.11$), heavy metal ($+1.06$), or indie and alternative rock ($+1.01$) marks out a high-affirmation respondent just as strongly as consuming the consecrated genres does. Dimension 1 is thus a \emph{general affirmation} axis: a gradient in the overall propensity to say yes across all modalities at once, ordering respondents from generalized non-engagement to generalized engagement with the genre system. Affirming the rarest modalities (e.g., consuming Opera or Reggae or thinking of Hip Hop and Heavy Metal fans as high status) receive the most extreme scores, as is typical of MCA \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44}.

The second dimension, shown in the category map (Figure~\ref{fig:categories}), organizes genres hierarchically rather than by modality. At one pole sit the ``yes'' categories of the consecrated, highbrow end of the genre system (big band $+0.79$, Broadway and show tunes $+0.77$, opera $+0.67$, classical $+0.67$, folk $+0.64$); at the other pole sit rap/hip-hop ($-1.05$ and $-0.98$ for consumption and preference), dance/club ($-0.95$), indie and alternative rock ($-0.94$), heavy metal ($-0.88$), and reggae ($-0.85$). Dimension 2 is therefore a \emph{highbrow--popular} axis that holds within each of the three modalities simultaneously---the same opposition that classical work in the field has located at the core of musical taste structures \citep{bourdieu1984distinction}. The individual factor maps (Figure~\ref{fig:individuals}) preview this axis's social anchoring: respondents' positions are strongly ordered by age, with the youngest cohort sitting toward the popular pole and the oldest toward the highbrow pole (Section~\ref{sec:social}). The vertical dimension of the map previews Dimension 3: the ``yes'' categories of all twenty strict status attributions lie clustered on one side of the origin, the visible signature of a distinct \emph{status-valuation} axis whose reading we take up in Section~\ref{sec:contrib}, once the modality contributions establish it as the evaluation modality's own.

\subsection{The Modality Structure: How Independent Are Preference, Engagement, and Evaluation?}

The central result bears on the first question posed above: whether the three modalities are redundant or partially independent. The RV coefficients (Table~\ref{tab:rv} and Figure~\ref{fig:rv}) answer it in favor of partial independence. The preference and consumption modalities are moderately linked ($RV = 0.32$): those who like a genre are somewhat more likely to have listened to it, but the two structures are far from interchangeable. By contrast, the evaluation modality is nearly orthogonal to both ($RV = 0.05$ with preference and $0.06$ with consumption).

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{RV coefficients between the three modality groups and the MFA.}
\label{tab:rv}
\input{tables/tab-rv}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.6\linewidth]{fig-rv} \caption{RV coefficients between taste modalities.}
\label{fig:rv}
\end{figure}

This near-orthogonality is the geometric signature of the pluralist conception of taste. Status attributions about who listens to a genre constitute a structurally independent dimension of taste that cannot be recovered from what people like or what they do. A respondent's evaluation profile is, to a first approximation, invisible in their preference and consumption profiles. Complex tastes---configurations in which the modalities disagree---are therefore not measurement noise or respondent inconsistency; they are the expected product of applying three weakly coupled measurement systems to the same objects.

\subsection{Which Modalities Drive Which Dimensions?}
\label{sec:contrib}

Table~\ref{tab:groups} reports the quantities that answer the second and third questions posed above: whether each modality actually participates in the compromise the MFA builds from them, and which modality organizes each dimension of the shared space. MFA's balancing weights---the inverses of the first eigenvalues of the separate analyses ($5.00$ for preference, $6.45$ for consumption, and $2.06$ for evaluation)---put the three modalities on equal footing despite the evaluation modality's much stronger internal first dimension ($\lambda_1 = 0.48$ versus $0.20$ and $0.15$).

\label{tab:groups}

\end{table}

\label{tab:partial-axes}
\input{tables/tab-partial-axes}
\end{table}

On the third question, the answer is that the dimensions are not modality-neutral. Preference and consumption dominate the first two dimensions (contributing $38\%$ and $40\%$ respectively to Dimension 1, and $41\%$ and $53\%$ to Dimension 2). The third dimension is different in kind: evaluation contributes $40.6\%$---nearly double its share of Dimension 1 ($21.6\%$) and almost six times its share of Dimension 2 ($7.0\%$)---while preference and consumption recede. The content of the dimension is unambiguous: \emph{every one} of the twenty strict high-status ``yes'' categories lies on the same (negative) side of Dimension 3 (mean coordinate $-0.63$; Figure~\ref{fig:categories}), against a positive pole anchored by consumption of the consecrated genres (opera $+0.90$, reggae $+0.65$, Latin/Salsa $+0.56$, big band $+0.52$). Dimension 3 is thus a distinct axis of the taste space organized by \emph{status valuation} rather than preference or engagement. The $Lg$ coefficients answer the participation question from the other direction: every modality leaves a detectable imprint on the compromise---none is present in name only---but unevenly. The link between evaluation and the MFA ($Lg = 0.75$) is much weaker than the links of preference ($1.80$) and consumption ($2.29$), and the cross-modality $Lg$ coefficients mirror the RV structure (preference--consumption $0.80$ versus $0.07$ and $0.11$ for the pairs involving evaluation).

The partial axes---each modality's own axes from the separate analyses, projected into the global space (Table~\ref{tab:partial-axes})---corroborate this reading from the side of the separate analyses.\footnote{The partial axis of a modality is one of its separate-analysis axes represented in the global space; its correlation with a global dimension is the Pearson correlation between respondents' coordinates on the two axes.} The first dimension is the axis of maximal consensus: the leading axis of all three separate analyses correlates strongly with it ($0.79$, $0.81$, and $0.60$ for preference, consumption, and evaluation). The highbrow--popular dimension is carried by the second axes of preference ($-0.89$) and consumption ($+0.89$) alone, with no evaluation axis coming close---the correlational counterpart of the evaluation modality's $7.0\%$ contribution. The status-valuation dimension, by contrast, is where the evaluation modality's dominant internal opposition is expressed ($-0.60$)---though that same axis correlates just as strongly with the general-affirmation dimension ($+0.60$), and the third axes of preference ($+0.57$) and consumption ($+0.60$) align with it as well: the dimension is evaluation-led but not evaluation-alone, as its $40.6\%$ contribution against $28.2\%$ and $31.2\%$ for the other two modalities already indicated.

\subsection{Operationalizing Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:antinomies}

We operationalize complex tastes geometrically: as the dispersion $W_s(i)$ of the individual's three partial points (Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}), read directly off the MFA representation. Ma's eight configurations provide a discrete complement to this measure; we examine it in Appendix~\ref{app:configurations} and borrow its vocabulary throughout.

The complex-taste scores quantify how much of each respondent's position in the taste space is modality disagreement. On the first three dimensions, the dispersion of partial points accounts for $51\%$, $51\%$, and $62\%$ of the average projected partial inertia, respectively: by geometry alone, disagreement between modalities contributes about as much to respondents' positions in the taste space as agreement does. On the third dimension, the pair-level decomposition locates the disagreement where the theory predicts: the preference--evaluation ($\rho = -0.28$ with the dimension) and consumption--evaluation ($\rho = -0.25$) pairs disagree most among respondents located at the pole anchored by the strict status attributions (the negative sign indicates that disagreement concentrates at that pole). Figure~\ref{fig:antinomy-map} colors the individual factor map by the complex-taste score on Dimension 1; the score is essentially unrelated to the two dimensions shown ($\rho = 0.01$ and $0.02$), so complex tastes are distributed across the hierarchical and status-valuation axes rather than concentrated in any region of the plane.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.7\linewidth]{fig-antinomy-map} \caption{Individual factor map (dimensions 2--3), colored by the geometric complex-taste score on Dimension 1 ($W_1$).}
\label{fig:antinomy-map}
\end{figure}

The two operationalizations also diverge in instructive ways (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}, Table~\ref{tab:antinomy}). The geometric complex-taste score on Dimension 1 tracks the total number of complex tastes ($\rho = 0.58$; $\rho = 0.46$ with the total dispersion across the first three dimensions), but its counterparts on Dimensions 2 and 3 do not ($0.11$ and $0.03$). The lesson is that geometric and combinatorial measures of complex tastes are related but not interchangeable: the dispersion of partial points captures \emph{how much} the modalities disagree overall, while the configuration counts capture \emph{which genres} the disagreement attaches to. They align where complex tastes are a matter of degree of engagement (Dimension 1) and diverge where they are a matter of hierarchical placement (Dimensions 2 and 3).

\subsection{The Social Sources of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:social}

To situate the sources of complex tastes socially, we project a set of respondent demographics---gender, race/ethnicity, age, education, parental education, household income, subjective social class, and census region---as supplementary variables onto the MFA representation. Supplementary variables do not influence the analysis: a category's coordinates are the barycenter of its members' positions in the common space, and the strength of each variable's association with each dimension is summarized by the correlation ratio $\eta^2$ (Tables~\ref{tab:eta} and \ref{tab:sup-coord}; Figure~\ref{fig:supplementary}).

The social anatomy of the taste space runs primarily through the highbrow--popular dimension. Age is the strongest single anchor ($\eta^2 = 0.35$), with a nearly monotone gradient: respondents aged 18--29 sit at $-0.76$ on Dimension 2, those 30--39 at $-0.46$, those 40--49 at $-0.20$, those 50--59 at $+0.26$, those 60--69 at $+0.76$, and those 70 and older at $+1.23$---the genre hierarchy doubles as an age hierarchy. Education traces the same axis monotonically (No diploma $-0.25$, HS/GED $-0.22$, some college $-0.10$, Associate's degree $-0.07$, BA $+0.08$, MA $+0.46$, professional or doctoral degree $+0.59$; $\eta^2 = 0.04$), as does subjective social class (Lower $-0.30$, Working $-0.22$, Middle $+0.23$, Upper $+0.22$; $\eta^2 = 0.05$), with household income and race/ethnicity following more weakly (Hispanic $-0.54$, Black $-0.32$, White $+0.21$). Gender and census region are negligible across all three dimensions.

The general-affirmation dimension is only weakly socially structured---no demographic variable exceeds $\eta^2 = 0.03$ on it---but the education pattern is instructive: the gradient is concentrated at the bottom of the credential distribution (No diploma $-0.54$, HS/GED $-0.31$) and flattens from some college upward ($+0.15$ to $+0.17$), indicating that generalized engagement with the genre system is most sharply differentiated at the entry into credentials rather than across their full range.

The status-valuation dimension, by contrast, has a social signature that is distinctly \emph{not} the education gradient. Education is nearly absent from it ($\eta^2 = 0.008$). Race/ethnicity is its strongest demographic correlate ($\eta^2 = 0.08$): Black ($+0.55$), Asian ($+0.26$), and Hispanic ($+0.24$) respondents sit toward the consecrated-consumption pole, while White respondents sit slightly toward the strict-attribution pole ($-0.19$). Self-described upper-class respondents sit far toward the consumption pole ($+0.68$, $n = 55$), as do children of college-educated parents ($+0.12$) and high-income respondents ($+0.14$). Whatever the status-valuation dimension captures, it is not reducible to credentialism: it partitions the population along lines that formal education barely touches, which is consistent with its geometric independence from the preference and consumption modalities established above.

\subsection{Who Has Complex Tastes?}
\label{sec:who}

The geometric measuring of complex tastes has one further advantage: $W_s(i)$ is a continuous, dimension-specific quantity, and can therefore serve directly as the outcome of a standard regression model---something the combinatorial count, a single coarse integer, does not allow. Table~\ref{tab:regression} reports OLS regressions of the three complex-taste scores on the same demographics projected as supplementary variables above. The headline result is the smallness of the associations: the full set of eight demographics accounts for $4.0\%$ of the variance in $W_1$, $3.1\%$ in $W_2$, and $2.2\%$ in $W_3$. Where respondents sit in the taste space is strongly socially patterned (Section~\ref{sec:social}); how much their modalities disagree is nearly socially unstructured. Complex tastes, on the geometric measure, are distributed across the social structure rather than concentrated within any of its segments.

The partial effects that do emerge are informative. Disagreement over engagement ($W_1$) is higher among respondents whose parents hold a BA ($+0.92$) and among those who identify as upper class ($+3.56$), and it declines with age ($-0.79$ at ages 30--39 through $-1.29$ at 70+, relative to the youngest cohort): modality disagreement over liking, listening, and valuing is, if anything, concentrated among the advantaged rather than the excluded. Disagreement over the genre hierarchy ($W_2$) is essentially an age effect: every intermediate cohort disagrees less than the youngest ($-0.52$ to $-1.01$), while the oldest cohort returns to the young level ($+0.08$)---the modalities align most tightly in late middle age. Disagreement over status valuation ($W_3$) follows race rather than class: respondents of more than one race disagree more ($+1.94$) and Asian respondents less ($-1.50$) than White respondents, while Black and Hispanic respondents are statistically indistinguishable from the White majority.

These findings are robust to a logarithmic transformation of the outcomes, which addresses the skew of the $W$ scores: the parental-education effect on $W_1$ (partial $F = 4.9$), the age effect on $W_2$ ($F = 7.5$), and the race effect on $W_3$ ($F = 2.7$) all persist, and the subjective-class effect on $W_1$ is concentrated in the upper category ($+0.45$ on the log scale). The same demographics also predict the pairwise disagreement components of Dimension 3: race is the only variable significantly associated with both preference--evaluation and consumption--evaluation disagreement (more-than-one-race respondents $+2.2$ and $+3.5$; Asian respondents $-2.2$ and $-2.3$), while preference--consumption disagreement is patterned by parental education ($+0.55$) and upper-class identification ($+1.08$). At the individual level, then, complex tastes are not the signature of any particular social location; they arise wherever the three weakly coupled measurement systems happen to diverge.

\subsection{The Duality: Genres as Targets of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:duality}

Complex tastes have a dual structure: individuals are \emph{sources} of complex tastes, and genres are \emph{targets}. To measure the target side, we transpose the analysis: individuals are now the twenty genres, and each modality block contains one binary variable per respondent---whether that respondent likes, listens to, or grants conjunctive high status to the genre. Respondents whose answers are constant across all twenty genres within a modality (who like nothing, listen to nothing, or credit no genre's fans with high status) define variables with an empty category; they contribute no genre discrimination and are dropped (83, 84, and 663 respondent-variables respectively). The transposition is not a mere rearrangement of the original solution. In simple correspondence analysis, the row and column clouds are dual, and the genre coordinates could be read off the original fit at no cost; but multiple correspondence analysis with a block structure breaks that duality. The category coordinates of the original analysis locate a genre through the composition of its audience---the barycenter of the respondents who affirm it---whereas the transposed analysis locates genres as objects, with distances computed over the respondent-indicators within each modality block. Because MFA weights each block by the inverse of the first eigenvalue of its separate analysis, and transposing changes the separate analyses, the balancing weights and hence the eigen-decomposition differ: the transposed dimensions are optimized for the dispersion of the genre cloud rather than the respondent cloud ($\lambda_1 = 2.31$ here against $1.67$ above). And statistics defined over the individuals of an analysis---RV coefficients and partial points among them---do not survive transposition: the genre-level RV coefficients and the modality-specific genre partial points reported below exist only in the transposed fit. The transposed MFA was implemented by direct application of the algorithm in \citet{pages2014mfa} and validated by reproducing the respondent-level \textsf{FactoMineR} solution: eigenvalues, global and partial coordinates, RV coefficients, and group contributions all agree to within $10^{-4}$.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-map} \caption{Genre map from the transposed MFA. Black points: genre compromise positions; colored points: modality partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its modality-specific positions).}
\label{fig:genre-map}
\end{figure}

The central result of the duality analysis is that, from the object side, the modalities \emph{agree}. The genre-level RV coefficients are $0.92$ (preference--consumption), $0.77$ (preference--evaluation), and $0.73$ (consumption--evaluation)---against $0.32$, $0.05$, and $0.06$ at the individual level. The disagreement that constitutes complex tastes is therefore not a property of the objects: the population that likes a genre, the population that listens to it, and the population that credits its fans with high status are, to a substantial approximation, the same population. What varies---and what generates complex tastes---is whether a given individual occupies all three positions with respect to a given genre at the same time. Modality independence is an individual-level achievement, not a genre-level partition.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Genre target profiles: percentage of respondents holding each genre in each of Ma's configurations ($N = 2{,}259$).}
\label{tab:genre-profile}
\input{tables/tab-genre-profile}
\end{table}

The transposed space is itself strongly structured ($\lambda_1 = 2.31$, $13.2\%$ of the inertia; $\lambda_2 = 2.13$, $12.1\%$). Its second dimension is a \emph{configuration axis}: genres are ordered by the complex-taste profiles they attract (Table~\ref{tab:genre-profile}). At the negative pole sit the mainstream genres that function as guilty-pleasure targets---the guilty-pleasure rate correlates $-0.90$ with the dimension---together with simple tastes ($-0.76$), distanced consumption ($-0.57$), and pre-acquired tastes ($-0.57$): classic rock/oldies ($-3.8$), top 40/pop ($-2.5$), country ($-2.0$), and mood/easy listening ($-1.3$). At the positive pole sit the consecrated genres that attract distant praise ($\rho = +0.59$): opera ($+2.3$), folk ($+1.4$), bluegrass ($+1.3$), and classical ($+0.8$)---genres whose fans are granted high status by respondents who neither like nor listen to them. The duality is asymmetric in exactly the way the theory of complex tastes anticipates: the prototypical guilty-pleasure genres are those least credited with high status, and the prototypical distant-praise genres are those least consumed. The first dimension opposes genres of devoted minority engagement (classical $-3.9$, Broadway/show tunes $-1.9$, opera $-1.6$; simple-taste and taste-pose rates load at $-0.51$ and $-0.78$) with genres of generalized non-engagement (rap/hip-hop $+2.6$, heavy metal $+1.6$, reggae $+1.6$; simple non-taste $+0.67$)---well-known genres held in simple non-taste by most respondents.

Finally, the partial points locate where the modalities disagree about specific objects despite their global agreement. On the third dimension, the evaluation partial points of the consecrated genres are displaced toward positive values relative to their preference and consumption partial points (classical: $+2.6$ for evaluation against $+1.0$ for preference and consumption; opera: $+2.0$ against $+0.0$ and $+0.2$), while country shows the reverse displacement (evaluation $-1.9$ against $-3.5$ and $-4.7$). Status attributions, in other words, are distributed across genres in a way that only partially tracks who likes and who listens---echoing, at the level of the objects, the modality independence established at the level of the sources.

\section{Discussion}

[DRAFT: The results establish three things. First, the three modalities of taste are empirically distinct structures, with evaluation nearly orthogonal to preference and consumption. Second, the shared space of taste is organized by a general-engagement gradient and a highbrow--popular hierarchy, both of which are visible in all modalities. Third, there exists a third-order dimension driven disproportionately by status evaluation---a candidate geometric locus for complex tastes. The operationalization of complex tastes is carried out in Section~\ref{sec:antinomies}, their social sources in Section~\ref{sec:social}, their individual-level correlates in Section~\ref{sec:who}, and the duality of sources and targets in Section~\ref{sec:duality}. The remaining steps are the robustness note comparing the inclusive and conjunctive evaluation codings, and full introductory and discussion prose.]

\section{The Combinatorial Measure: Ma's Eight Configurations}
\label{app:configurations}

The geometric measure locates complex tastes continuously in the common space. As a discrete complement, each genre--respondent pair can be classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex configurations.

Complex tastes are the statistical norm of this taste culture, not the exception. Figure~\ref{fig:configurations} reports the mean number of genres held in each configuration: the average respondent holds $9.6$ of the $20$ genres in a complex configuration, and only $19$ of $2{,}259$ respondents hold no complex configuration at all. The most frequent complex configuration is the \emph{justified abstention} ($2.8$ genres on average), followed by \emph{distant praise} ($2.6$) and the \emph{guilty pleasure} ($2.2$): respondents routinely like genres whose fans they do not credit with high status, grant high status to genres they neither like nor consume, and enjoy-and-consume genres whose fans they do not so credit. The taste pose ($1.5$) and the rare variants---distanced consumption ($0.4$) and the pre-acquired taste ($0.2$)---are comparatively infrequent, while the simple non-taste ($8.6$) is the single largest configuration.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.75\linewidth]{fig-configurations} \caption{Taste portfolios: mean number of genres held in each of Ma's eight configurations, per respondent. Orange: complex configurations; grey: simple ones.}
\label{fig:configurations}
\end{figure}

Table~\ref{tab:antinomy} relates the configuration counts to the MFA dimensions and to the geometric complex-taste scores; the discrete types turn out to have distinct geometric signatures. Distant praise remains strongly located on the status-valuation dimension ($\rho = -0.66$, the pole anchored by the strict attributions) and tilts toward the highbrow pole of Dimension 2 ($\rho = 0.22$): distant praise concentrates in consecrated genres whose fans' status respondents grant without liking or consuming them---the survey analogue of the unread bestseller. Guilty pleasures lean the opposite way in the genre hierarchy ($\rho = -0.34$ with the highbrow pole, that is, toward the popular pole) and occupy the opposite pole of Dimension 3 from distant praise ($\rho = 0.46$), with justified abstentions joining them there ($\rho = 0.50$). Taste poses are found among respondents high on the general-affirmation dimension who favor the highbrow pole ($\rho = 0.48$ and $0.30$).
